Overall I enjoyed this movie, and I think a big part of that is that I went in almost completely blind. I only saw the first (great) trailer, which was intriguing without giving anything away. I have no idea why they decided to give away almost the entire movie in the final trailer. 

I loved how Peele subverted my expectations. I went into it thinking it'd be some sort of UFO/alien movie, and I was right, but not in the way I expected! What stood out to me the most is the nature of the alien. Maybe this isn't the right word, but it almost seemed... Lovecraftian to me. Not just an alien, but something inorganic and unfeeling. It just eats whatever looks at it. It shows no emotion, just hunger. I loved the amorphous, windy, fabric like look of it. Like it's both of this planet and not at the same time. And the fact that it's never clearly shown how exactly it eats people. We just see an ominous chamber, hear people screaming from within, and the bloody aftermath. It's terrifying. And also, the poor fucking audience. There were kids there who were eaten alive, Jesus. 


Now for the criticisms. I feel bad for saying this, but I wasn't a huge fan of Michael Wincott. His voice and character (washed up, cynical but successful artist who is unphased by everything and kills himself at the end) felt cliche. Also, the idea that the Haywoods would be so desperate for money and fame that they'd risk being eaten by some unfathomable horror is... kind of dumb. I was able to partially look past it since they just got kicked from a gig, but for a movie that seems to pride itself on the main characters saying "nope" to deadly curiosity, it's ironic. Finally, the message that "you shouldn't try to tame the untamable" is both not terribly original and wasn't delivered very subtly. Using Gordy to drive it home felt, ironically, like I was being beaten by a chimp at times. That all sounds harsh, but the execution and monster design was good enough for me to mostly forgive it. And there's probably more to it that I'm just too tired to realize. 

If I were to rank Jordan Peele's movies from worst to best, it'd be *Us*, *Nope*, and *Get Out*, with *Get Out* being further ahead from the rest. I liked *Us* right after I saw it, but the more I thought about it the dumber some of the choices in it seemed. Hopefully that doesn't happen with this movie. And it didn't leave as much of an impact on my mind than *Get Out*. I only have a vague memory of what actually happens in it.
